etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English depressen, from Old French depresser, from Latin dēpressus, perfect participle of dēprimō (“to press down, to weigh down”), from dē- (“off, away, down, out”) +‎ premō (“to press”).

quote.citation: 1947 January and February, Cecil J. Allen, “British Locomotive Practice and Performance”, in Railway Magazine, page 39:
quote.text: As to the fireman, the sight of him at work, swinging round with his shovelful of coal and at the same moment lightly depressing his right heel and so working the pedal which causes the steam-operated firedoors to open like magic in front of the shovel, was always a pleasure.

definitions.definition: To make depressed, sad or bored.
(economics) To cause a depression or a decrease in parts of the economy.
To bring down or humble; to abase (pride, etc.).
(mathematics) To reduce (an equation) in a lower degree.
